query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Differences in mechanical properties among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary/ternary subsets are primarily governed by variations in the local stacking fault energy (SFE) landscape induced by element-specific chemical short‐range order. In alloys with fewer constituents, enhanced short‐range order creates larger local SFE fluctuations that promote planar slip and twinning, whereas in the equiatomic quinary alloy the chemical disorder homogenizes the SFE distribution, leading to a different balance between dislocation glide and twinning.
generation.material_initial_state: Thermomechanically processed, single-phase FCC equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its corresponding quaternary/ternary subsets with controlled grain size and minimal secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of the constituent count (quinary to quaternary and ternary combinations) while keeping processing parameters fixed.
generation.conditions: Room temperature deformation tests under controlled strain rate in an inert atmosphere; complementary microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM and atom probe tomography) post-deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Local stacking fault energy variations regulated by the degree of chemical short‐range order.
generation.mechanism: Element-specific interactions drive the formation (or frustration) of short-range order, which in turn modulates the effective local SFE. Lower elemental diversity (in quaternary or ternary alloys) can promote stronger local chemical ordering, resulting in higher local SFE variations that favor deformation mechanisms such as planar slip and twinning, altering the yield strength and work-hardening behavior relative to the chemically more disordered equiatomic quinary alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the equiatomic quinary baseline, selected quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit measurable differences in yield strength and ductility. Specifically, increased chemical order in lower-component alloys is expected to produce sharper SFE variations, promoting twinning or more localized dislocation slip which may increase work hardening and strength, albeit potentially at the cost of ductility.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties and deformation mode observations of the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy processed under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single-phase, thermomechanically processed FCC multi-principal element alloys tested at room temperature in an inert atmosphere where oxidation and phase transformation are negligible.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contribution of local SFE modulation versus other factors such as lattice distortions or solute atomic size effects remains uncertain, and the degree to which short-range order can be reliably controlled across different alloy compositions is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys and selected quaternary/ternary subsets under identical thermomechanical processing conditions. Conduct room temperature tensile tests while simultaneously performing TEM and atom probe tomography to examine local chemical ordering and measure stacking fault energy indicators (e.g., twin thickness, partial dislocation spacing).
measurements: Yield strength and ductility from tensile tests
Local microstructural features such as twin density and dislocation configurations
Chemical short-range order statistics obtained from atom probe tomography
Indirect stacking fault energy estimations via analysis of twin structures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanical property differences (yield strength, ductility, work-hardening behavior) between the equiatomic quinary alloy and its lower-component subsets cannot be correlated with measurable differences in the local stacking fault energy landscape or chemical short-range order (i.e., if no consistent trend is observed between refined SFE-related microstructural features and the deformation behavior), then the hypothesis that local SFE modulation via chemical order governs the mechanical-property differences would be falsified.
